title: In the same multi-echo fMRI run, cortical region timescales were 12-18% shorter at 13 ms than at 30 ms echo time after a high-pass filter, but changed little after 0.01-0.1 Hz band-pass (21 studies)
abstract: In the same fMRI run, the timescale of cortical regional fMRI signals was longer at longer echo time (TE) when the analysis kept frequencies above 0.1 Hz, but changed little after a 0.01-0.1 Hz band-pass filter. This is important because studies compare these timescales ("intrinsic neural timescales") between groups, sites and protocols, and TE and filters differ between studies. We used ReadyNeuro, a corpus of minimally preprocessed OpenNeuro fMRI on a 1-s time grid. It keeps each echo of a multi-echo scan as a separate run. Thus the echoes of one run have the same brain activity, head motion and physiology, and only TE is different. The timescale is the sum of the positive autocorrelation values of a signal at 1-s steps. After a 0.01 Hz high-pass filter, the median timescale of 200 cortical regions increased by 0.23 s for each doubling of TE in 7 discovery studies (70 people, rest; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.33). In a pre-registered test in 14 held-out studies (174 runs in 20 study or protocol units, rest and task), it increased by 0.21 s (0.17 to 0.24). The timescale at a TE of about 13 ms was 12% and 18% shorter than at about 30 ms (0.6 to 0.8 of the standard deviation between people), and it did not change above 30 ms. 7 of 8 pre-registered tests passed. An independent review then found, and we confirmed on both sets, that the effect depends on the analysis: after a 0.01-0.1 Hz band-pass filter it was small (0.07 and 0.03 s per doubling), after a 0.008-0.08 Hz band-pass it was absent, and in the mean signal of the whole cortex it became negative after band-pass filtering together with regression of white-matter and CSF signals. Thus most of the TE-dependent part is above 0.1 Hz. There, the TE-independent part of the signal (S0: inflow, head motion, breathing, scanner instability) has relatively more power than the BOLD part, as earlier work showed for its spectrum. White thermal noise explained about one third of the regional change from 13 to 30 ms. Limits: the pipeline results were not pre-registered; we did not use breathing, pulse or motion recordings; there was one run per person; between single-echo studies, TE changes too little to test the effect.

display.caption: Median timescale of 200 cortical regions at each echo, relative to the echo nearest 30 ms of the same run, after (a) a 0.01 Hz high-pass filter (pre-registered) and (b) a 0.01-0.1 Hz band-pass filter. Each line is the mean over the people of one study or scan protocol. Blue: 7 discovery studies; orange: 20 confirmation units.

Change in timescale per doubling of echo time (random effects over studies, 95% CI) for seven analysis pipelines, for the median region (blue) and the mean cortical signal (orange). Left: discovery; right: confirmation. Linear detrend only in discovery (-1.32 and -2.00) is outside the axis.

Change in timescale per doubling of echo time (0.01 Hz high-pass) in 8 scan protocols of the same people (ds004499: 6; ds006926: 2), for the mean cortical signal (orange) and the median region (blue). Mean and 95% CI over 10 people. MB: multiband factor; FA: flip angle in degrees.
